articles.headline: Treasury Sanctions Iran's Shadow Banking Network, Targeting Exchange Houses and Front Companies Across Middle East and Asia
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has imposed sanctions on over two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front companies, and officials, asserting that these entities form the backbone of Iran's shadow banking system. This network is allegedly used by Tehran to circumvent comprehensive sanctions, facilitating the movement of export earnings and payments for imports.

The designations, announced on November 23, 2026, target firms located in Iran, Dubai, Hong Kong, and Turkey. This action is part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' a campaign initiated by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on August 24, 2026, with the goal of cutting off revenue streams supporting the Iranian government.

Among the entities listed are Rahbar Bazargani Nesim Baharan Qeshm Company, identified as the 'rahbar company' for Iran's Bank Sarmayeh, along with three of its senior officials. Additionally, two Iranian exchange houses, Mina Fashki and Partners Exchange Company and Mellat Exchange Company, were designated, including their owners and officials. Ten front companies, primarily based in Dubai and Hong Kong, were also sanctioned for processing cross-border payments for Iranian clients.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran Designations and Publishes Updated Cuba Sanctions FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran designations on November 20, 2026. While specific details of the designated entities were not immediately released in the initial announcement, these actions signify a continued focus on applying pressure to Iran through economic sanctions.

In addition to the Iran-related measures, OFAC also issued updated Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) concerning Cuba sanctions. These FAQs aim to provide clarity and guidance to individuals and entities regarding compliance with the complex regulatory framework surrounding transactions involving Cuba.

The issuance of new FAQs often indicates a need to address evolving scenarios or common misunderstandings in the application of sanctions, helping to ensure that U.S. persons and businesses understand their obligations and avoid potential violations.

articles.headline: OFAC Targets Narcotics and Cyber Actors, Issues New Illicit Drugs GL, and Amends Russia-Related Guidance
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a series of designations on November 19, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and cyber-related illicit activities. These actions underscore the U.S. government's commitment to disrupting global criminal networks that pose threats to national security and financial stability.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued a new Illicit Drugs General License, which aims to facilitate certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under sanctions programs related to illicit drug trafficking. This license is intended to support legitimate activities while maintaining pressure on illicit actors.

Furthermore, OFAC issued an amended Russia-related General License and updated Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs). These revisions likely provide additional guidance and potentially modify existing authorizations or prohibitions concerning transactions involving Russia, reflecting the dynamic nature of sanctions policy in response to ongoing geopolitical developments.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Counter Terrorism Designations to Disrupt Terrorist Financing
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new counter terrorism designations on November 18, 2026. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to combat global terrorism by targeting individuals and entities that provide financial, material, or technological support to terrorist organizations.

The designations aim to disrupt terrorist financing networks and limit their ability to operate internationally. By identifying and sanctioning these actors, OFAC seeks to isolate them from the U.S. financial system and broader international commerce.
These measures reinforce the U.S. government's commitment to protecting national security and working with international partners to counter the threats posed by terrorism worldwide.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Dual Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a dual set of designations on November 13, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in both counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. This combined approach highlights the interconnectedness of various illicit networks and the comprehensive strategy employed by the U.S. government to combat them.

These designations aim to disrupt the financial and operational capabilities of organizations engaged in drug trafficking and those supporting terrorist acts. By targeting both aspects simultaneously, OFAC seeks to maximize the impact of its sanctions programs.
The actions underscore the ongoing commitment to protecting the U.S. financial system from abuse by illicit actors and to safeguarding national security interests against a range of global threats.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Update to Iran Designation List
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) published an update to its Iran designation list on November 9, 2026. These updates typically involve additions, removals, or modifications to the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List or other sanctions lists related to Iran.

Such updates are a routine part of OFAC's ongoing efforts to maintain the effectiveness and accuracy of its sanctions programs. They reflect new intelligence, changes in circumstances, or administrative adjustments.

Entities and individuals involved in international transactions are advised to regularly check OFAC's updated lists to ensure compliance and avoid engaging in prohibited activities with sanctioned parties.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-Related Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 6, 2026. These actions are part of the U.S. government's broader strategy to exert economic pressure on Iran, targeting various sectors and individuals perceived to be supporting the Iranian regime's destabilizing activities.

The specific details of the newly designated entities or individuals were not immediately available in the initial announcement, but such designations typically aim to disrupt financial networks, procurement efforts, or other activities deemed contrary to U.S. foreign policy objectives.

These ongoing designations underscore the U.S. commitment to its maximum pressure campaign against Iran, seeking to limit the regime's access to resources and its ability to fund regional proxies and illicit programs.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber and Transnational Criminal Organizations, Imposes Cuba Sanctions, and Publishes Determination
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a series of designations on November 5, 2026, targeting cyber-related actors and transnational criminal organizations. These actions aim to combat malicious cyber activities and disrupt the financial infrastructure of criminal enterprises operating across borders.

In addition to these global designations, OFAC also imposed new sanctions related to Cuba and published a Cuba-related determination. These measures reflect the U.S. government's continued policy towards Cuba, which often involves restricting financial transactions and trade to pressure the Cuban government.
The publication of a determination typically provides the legal basis or specific criteria for the new Cuba sanctions, offering clarity on the scope and application of these restrictive measures.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran Sanctions, Updates Listings, Issues Alert, and Amends Venezuela GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 4, 2026, alongside updates to existing Iran-related listings. These actions are part of a continuous effort to enhance the effectiveness of sanctions targeting Iran's various illicit activities.

In a significant move, OFAC also published an Iran-related OFAC Alert, which typically warns financial institutions and other entities about specific evasion tactics or heightened risks associated with transactions involving Iran. Such alerts are crucial for maintaining vigilance against sanctions circumvention.

Furthermore, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and an accompanying Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). These revisions likely adjust existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Venezuela, reflecting ongoing policy assessments and aiming to provide clearer guidance to stakeholders.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the issuance of an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026. General Licenses typically authorize categories of transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under a specific sanctions program, without the need for individual applications.

Amendments to General Licenses can broaden or narrow the scope of authorized activities, often in response to evolving policy considerations or practical implementation challenges. These changes are important for businesses and individuals engaged in permitted transactions with Iran.
Stakeholders are advised to review the amended General License carefully to ensure ongoing compliance with U.S. sanctions regulations concerning Iran.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Settles with OFAC for $1,529,685 Over Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based cloud networking solutions provider, has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to settle potential civil liability for nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations. The settlement was announced by OFAC on October 27, 2026.

The violations occurred between September 2018 and March 2022, when Extreme exported networking equipment and related services from the United States to Joint Stock Company (JSC) Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), a Russian defense manufacturer. MMZA was blocked by operation of law due to being majority-owned by the designated JSC Concern Almaz Antey.
OFAC determined that the apparent violations were egregious and voluntarily self-disclosed. A parallel non-prosecution agreement was also reached with the Department of Justice on the same day.

articles.headline: Bank of America Settles with OFAC for $11,662,930 in Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to pay $11,662,930 to settle 475 apparent violations of various U.S. sanctions programs. The settlement was announced by OFAC on October 13, 2026, as part of a coordinated enforcement action with FinCEN and the OCC.

The violations, which occurred between September 2021 and April 2025, involved transactions totaling approximately $14.8 million across sanctions programs related to Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

OFAC classified the violations as non-egregious and mostly not voluntarily disclosed. The apparent violations stemmed from failures in the bank's sanctions screening program, including issues with vendor data, filter updates, alert prioritization, and human error.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Fined $175,015 by OFAC for Counter Narcotics Sanctions Violations
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, a California-based freight forwarder, has agreed to pay $175,015 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC counter narcotics sanctions and reporting obligations. The settlement was announced on October 9, 2026.

The apparent violations occurred when Pegasus arranged for the shipment of a sugar packet-filling machine from a designated Chinese supplier, Youli Technology Development Co., Ltd., which had been sanctioned under Executive Order 14059 for its involvement in producing counterfeit pills. Pegasus failed to identify the designated supplier due to deficiencies in its compliance review and program.

OFAC also cited Pegasus for initially failing to respond fully to an administrative subpoena for six months. The settlement amount reflects OFAC's determination that the conduct was non-egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed, but also acknowledges extensive remedial measures taken by Pegasus.

articles.headline: Individual Settles with OFAC for $1,427,230 in Sanctions Violations
body: An individual has agreed to pay $1,427,230 to settle potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations. The settlement was announced on September 10, 2026.

Details regarding the specific sanctions program and the nature of the violations were not immediately made public in the summary, but such penalties underscore OFAC's commitment to enforcing sanctions against individuals who engage in prohibited transactions.
This enforcement action serves as a reminder that individuals, not just corporations, are subject to OFAC regulations and can face significant penalties for non-compliance.

articles.headline: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. Pays $60,764 for Iran Sanctions Violations by Italian Subsidiary
body: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc., a Wisconsin-based manufacturer of weighing equipment, has agreed to pay $60,764 to settle its and its Italian subsidiary's potential civil liability for eight apparent violations of OFAC sanctions on Iran. The settlement was announced on August 12, 2026.

The violations occurred between July 2019 and November 2021, when Rice Lake's Italian subsidiary, Dini Argeo S.r.l., exported weighing equipment to Iran through a distributor in the United Arab Emirates, despite knowing the goods were ultimately destined for an end-user in Iran.

OFAC determined that these apparent violations were non-egregious and voluntarily self-disclosed. The case highlights the importance of robust oversight of foreign subsidiaries to ensure compliance with U.S. sanctions.

articles.headline: FTI Consulting, Inc. Settles with OFAC for $1,050,000 Over Russia Sanctions Violations
body: FTI Consulting, Inc., a Washington, D.C.-based international advisory firm, has agreed to pay $1,050,000 to settle its potential civil liability for six apparent violations of OFAC sanctions targeting Russia's financial sector. The settlement was announced on June 1, 2026.

Between April 2019 and May 2021, FTI indirectly dealt in prohibited debt of VTB Bank OAO, a Russian state-owned bank on OFAC's Sectoral Sanctions Identification List. FTI's exposure arose from invoices that VTB was ultimately responsible for paying, which effectively extended new debt with a maturity beyond the 14-day limit.

OFAC determined that FTI's conduct was non-egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed. The case underscores that indirect dealings through third parties do not necessarily circumvent sanctions prohibitions.

articles.headline: Adani Enterprises Limited Fined $275,000,000 by OFAC for Iran Sanctions Violations
body: Adani Enterprises Limited (AEL), a diversified multinational company headquartered in India, has agreed to pay $275,000,000 to settle its potential civil liability for 32 apparent violations of OFAC sanctions on Iran. The settlement was announced on May 18, 2026.

From November 2023 to June 2025, AEL purchased shipments of liquified petroleum gas (LPG) from a Dubai-based trader, despite red flags indicating the LPG actually originated from Iran. AEL caused U.S. financial institutions to process 32 U.S. dollar-denominated payments totaling approximately $192,104,044 for these shipments.

OFAC determined that AEL's apparent violations were egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed. However, the settlement amount reflects AEL's remedial measures taken after discovering the conduct and its cooperation with OFAC's investigation.

articles.headline: TradeStation Securities, Inc. Settles with OFAC for $1,110,661 Over Multiple Sanctions Violations
body: TradeStation Securities, Inc., a Florida-headquartered brokerage firm, has agreed to pay $1,110,661 to settle its potential civil liability for 481 apparent violations of multiple sanctions programs. The settlement was announced by OFAC on March 17, 2026.

For nearly a year, from June 2021 to June 2022, TradeStation provided investment services to customers located in Iran, Syria, and the Crimea region of Ukraine, enabling them to execute securities-related transactions.

The apparent violations stemmed from compliance control failures, including issues with geo-blocking controls and a lack of adequate testing by sanctions compliance personnel. OFAC determined the violations were non-egregious and voluntarily self-disclosed, and the settlement reflects the significant remedial measures implemented by TradeStation.

articles.headline: Individual Settles with OFAC for $3,777,000 in Syrian Sanctions Violations
body: An individual has agreed to pay $3,777,000 to settle potential civil liability for 20 apparent violations of the Syrian Sanctions Regulations. The settlement was announced by OFAC on February 25, 2026.

The violations occurred between 2018 and 2021 and involved a U.S. citizen residing abroad. The specific nature of the transactions was not detailed in the summary, but the substantial penalty highlights the serious consequences for individuals who violate U.S. sanctions programs.

This enforcement action underscores OFAC's broad reach in enforcing sanctions against U.S. persons, regardless of their location, and emphasizes the importance of understanding and adhering to all applicable sanctions regulations.

articles.headline: IMG Academy, LLC Settles with OFAC for $1,720,000 Over Counternarcotics Sanctions Violations
body: IMG Academy, LLC, a U.S.-based academic and athletic training institution, has agreed to pay $1,720,000 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Sanctions Regulations. The settlement was announced by OFAC on February 12, 2026.

Over a five-year period, IMG Academy entered into tuition enrollment agreements with two individuals designated under the Kingpin Act and processed 89 related financial transactions for the benefit of the designees' children. OFAC found that routine due diligence, such as screening contracting parties or payors, would have revealed that the individuals' names matched entries on the SDN List.

OFAC cited aggravating factors including reckless disregard for sanctions requirements and actual knowledge of transactional activity with sanctioned parties. Mitigating factors included IMG's lack of prior violations, substantial cooperation, and the implementation of a formal sanctions compliance program.

articles.headline: Global Central Banks Grapple with Persistent Inflation Amidst Divergent Growth Forecasts
body: Central banks worldwide are continuing to navigate a complex economic landscape characterized by persistent inflationary pressures and increasingly divergent growth outlooks. While some economies show signs of resilience, others face headwinds from geopolitical tensions and tighter financial conditions.

The U.S. Federal Reserve, European Central Bank, and Bank of England are all closely monitoring inflation data, with market analysts anticipating further commentary on potential interest rate adjustments in upcoming policy meetings. The challenge remains balancing inflation control with supporting economic activity.

Emerging markets, in particular, are facing unique pressures, including currency volatility and capital outflows, as global interest rate differentials widen. This divergence in economic performance and policy responses is creating a fragmented global financial environment.

articles.headline: Oil Prices Surge on Renewed Supply Concerns and Geopolitical Tensions
body: Global oil prices experienced a significant surge this week, driven by renewed concerns over supply disruptions and escalating geopolitical tensions in key producing regions. Benchmark crude futures rose sharply, impacting energy markets worldwide.

Analysts point to a combination of factors, including unexpected production outages and heightened rhetoric from major oil-producing nations, as contributing to the upward pressure on prices. The volatility underscores the fragility of global energy supply chains.

The increase in oil prices is expected to have a ripple effect across various industries, potentially exacerbating inflationary pressures and impacting consumer spending as winter approaches in the Northern Hemisphere.

The international community has expressed deep concern over the deteriorating security situation, with calls for an immediate cessation of hostilities and a return to dialogue to address the underlying issues fueling the conflict.

articles.headline: OCC Imposes Record $750 Million Penalty on Bank of America for AML Failures
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) imposed a record $750 million civil money penalty on Bank of America, N.A. on October 13, 2026, for widespread anti-money laundering (AML) and sanctions failures. This penalty was part of a coordinated action with FinCEN and OFAC, resulting in over $1.21 billion in combined penalties against the bank.

The OCC's action cited a deficient and ineffective Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and AML compliance program, highlighting a pattern of compliance breakdowns that the bank allegedly minimized rather than adequately addressed. The penalty is the largest ever imposed by the OCC.

Bank of America admitted to willful BSA violations, including failing to maintain an AML program meeting minimum requirements, neglecting due diligence on foreign correspondent accounts, and failing to file Suspicious Activity Reports in a timely manner, which resulted in the late reporting of over $5 billion in suspicious activity.

articles.headline: BIS Imposes New Export Controls on Advanced AI Chips and Remote Access to Overseas Data Centers
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued an interim final rule (IFR) on November 16, 2026, which became effective upon publication in the Federal Register on November 19, 2026. This rule introduces new export controls on advanced computing items, including advanced semiconductors, and restricts remote access to computing power in certain foreign data centers.

The IFR formally rescinds the previous 'AI Diffusion Rule' and imposes a new destination-based license requirement for exports, reexports, or in-country transfers of advanced computing items to five additional countries: Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. BIS states these countries present a 'higher-than-normal risk of diversion.'

Furthermore, the rule establishes a new end-use-based license requirement for advanced computing items destined for non-U.S. data centers that provide remote access to a 'significant volume of compute power' to end users headquartered in Macau or a Country Group D:5 destination (including China). This aims to prevent circumvention of existing controls on physical shipments of advanced semiconductors.
articles.source: U.S. Department of Commerce BIS / Federal Register

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Extension of the Suspension of Expansion of End-User Controls for Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is extending the suspension of the interim final rule (IFR), "Expansion of End-User Controls to Cover Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities." The suspension was set to end November 9, 2026. This final rule extends the suspension through January 10, 2027.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
